balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For PPL Corporation: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For PPL Corporation: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For PPL Corporation: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For PPL Corporation: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For PPL Corporation: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For PPL Corporation: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For PPL Corporation: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For PPL Corporation: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For PPL Corporation: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue

segmentNetIncome.title: Segment net income by jurisdiction
segmentNetIncome.content:
PPL operates three state-regulated utilities, each a separate rate case: Kentucky (LG&E/KU, vertically integrated electric and gas), Pennsylvania (PPL Electric, transmission & distribution only, no owned generation) and Rhode Island Energy (electric and gas, acquired from National Grid in 2022).

For PPL Corporation: Kentucky is consistently the largest earner on the biggest rate base; Rhode Island is the smallest segment and its net income fell in FY2025 even as its rate base grew, which is the segment to watch for a rate-case outcome lagging investment.

What to watch:

  • Whether each segment's earned ROE is tracking its authorized ROE (a shortfall means the next rate case asks for more)
  • Rhode Island's net income trend versus its rate base growth
  • Any shift in which segment carries the group's capex-driven growth

rateBaseSegment.title: Rate base by jurisdiction
rateBaseSegment.content:
Rate base is the capital investment a regulator allows the utility to earn a return on; it is the asset the authorized ROE is applied to, and its growth (driven by grid modernization and reliability capex) is the primary driver of regulated-utility earnings growth.

For PPL Corporation: all three jurisdictions are growing rate base, funding the company's multi-year capex plan; Kentucky and Pennsylvania are the two largest bases and the segments most of the capex program flows through.

What to watch:

  • Rate base CAGR versus the company's disclosed capex plan
  • Whether rate base growth is converting into segment net income growth (see the net income chart) -- a gap signals regulatory lag or a disallowed return

electricDeliveriesSegment.title: Electric deliveries by jurisdiction
electricDeliveriesSegment.content:
Electric deliveries (GWh) is the physical demand each segment serves -- the volume driver behind revenue in a business where price is set by rate case, not by the market.

For PPL Corporation: Pennsylvania delivers the most volume by far (PPL Electric is a dense, built-out distribution territory), while Kentucky and Rhode Island are smaller and more capacity-constrained. For a regulated utility, volume growth matters less than rate base growth -- it mainly signals load growth (data centers, electrification) that could support the next rate case.

What to watch:

  • Any acceleration from large-load customers (e.g. data centers) in Pennsylvania or Kentucky
  • Weather-driven swings versus the underlying trend (annual data only, so seasonality is already averaged out)
